title: Down-hand Welding — Theory and Safety Awareness
objective: Recognise at knowledge level what the down-hand welding position means, how the named welding-process families relate to this position, and why approved procedures, quality requirements and safety controls govern practical welding work.

curriculum_traceability.knowledge_topic: KM-06-KT05 — Gas, Arc, TIG, MIG welding in a down hand position
curriculum_traceability.primary_source: QCTO occupational curriculum hosted by CHIETA — Curriculum-6.pdf

safety_boundary: Knowledge and safety-awareness only. This lesson does not teach welding setup, machine or gas settings, ignition, electrode or consumable selection, torch or electrode movement, welding sequence, joint preparation procedures, or how to perform a weld. Practical welding belongs in authorised occupational training under competent supervision.

sections.heading: 1. What down-hand welding means
sections.body: Down-hand describes a welding position in which the work and weld orientation allow the welding operation to be performed from above the joint. At knowledge level, the important point is recognising the position and its relationship to the approved drawing, procedure and process.

sections.heading: 2. Welding-process families
sections.body: The occupational curriculum associates gas, arc, TIG and MIG welding with this knowledge topic. Learners should recognise these as different process families and understand that each has its own equipment, consumables, controls and approved applications.

sections.heading: 3. Position matters
sections.body: Welding position affects how a welding task is classified and controlled. The required position must therefore be identified from the applicable job information and approved procedure rather than assumed.

sections.heading: 4. Controlled information comes first
sections.body: Drawings, welding symbols, specifications, codes, data sheets and approved procedures communicate the technical requirements for welding work. At knowledge level, learners should understand that these requirements govern the work and take priority over informal practice or guesswork.

sections.heading: 5. Safety remains essential
sections.body: Welding can involve serious hazards including heat, intense light, fumes, electrical energy, hot material and fire risk. Practical welding therefore requires appropriate training, workplace controls, suitable protective measures and competent supervision.

sections.heading: 6. Quality is assessed against requirements
sections.body: A completed weld is judged against applicable quality requirements rather than appearance alone. Learners should recognise that inspection and testing may be required and that unacceptable conditions must be dealt with through the authorised workplace process.

sections.heading: 7. Knowledge is not practical authorisation
sections.body: Understanding welding positions and process families prepares a learner for supervised occupational development. It does not establish practical competence or permission to operate welding equipment independently.

sections.heading: 8. Stop and refer
sections.body: If the required welding position, process, drawing, specification, material information or approved procedure is unclear, stop and refer the matter to a competent trainer or supervisor before practical work is attempted.
